episodes.title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
episodes.description:
A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it.

The second test defines the level of automation inside a named workflow. AI attributed work and an autonomously completed task are different claims; the straight through completion rate needs a boundary that a buyer can inspect. The third test examines evaluation. A model judging another model's output is useful evidence only within its limits, and agreement with an automated rubric can diverge from a domain expert's assessment. Abelhad turns those checks into an economic question: what is the cost per accepted autonomous task after model costs, human review, escalation and rework? Failures belong in the denominator and the cost account. Public examples and a brief anonymous evaluation illustrate the framework rather than establish a general automation rate or a causal explanation for a company's failure. The takeaway is a practical diligence conversation that connects the deck's language to observable work, credible evaluation and the operating cost behind the claim.

episodes.title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part — Steve Jamison, Jellyfish
episodes.description:
AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. The largest cost in that calculation remains salary. These are observational comparisons, rather than proof that token spending caused the throughput change or that companies realized equivalent cash savings.

Jamison compares organizations with different levels of AI spending and then examines developers' weeks with and without heavier agent skill use. The analysis asks whether additional output spreads the salary allocation across enough work to outweigh the higher token bill. He also considers quality and work size: reverts offer one limited signal, while lines of code and pull request counts cannot by themselves establish customer value. A larger or more numerous set of changes may still need review, maintenance and evidence that it solves the right problem. The useful management question is therefore broader than whether the AI invoice went up. Teams need a consistent view of total engineering cost, output and quality before choosing where to encourage adoption or constrain spending. The talk provides a way to reason about that tradeoff while leaving causal attribution, economic value and the limits of output proxies open to scrutiny.

episodes.title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
episodes.description:
An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case.

Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies.

episodes.title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
episodes.description:
A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate.

When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a claim that the illustrative bank project shipped or that a checklist guarantees approval.

episodes.title: Every Building Is a Balance Sheet: Spatial Memory for Real-World Assets — Jordi Spranger, Spranic
episodes.description:
Two scans of the same kitchen reveal that three chairs have moved. The change can be queried against the captured scene, with a reference back to the observation. Jordi Spranger demonstrates the idea behind Spranic's spatial memory: turn a walk through a building into a record of its objects, relationships and changes over time. A conference hall scan provides a second example. Instead of leaving the evidence scattered across photographs and PDFs, the system stores a semantic representation in a graph that can connect observations from repeat visits. Questions such as where to find a radiator or a drinking glass become queries against that representation.

Spranger frames the problem around the gap between frequently updated financial records and infrequently updated knowledge of the buildings underneath them. He explains how an off the shelf sensor captures a space, how repeat walks align along a timeline and how object changes can feed downstream workflows. Maintenance, interior design, robotics and insurance are proposed uses of the same underlying asset record. For insurance, he sketches an initial inspection and renewal comparison that could inform a more specific policy. These are proposed applications, rather than demonstrated insurer deployments or measured premium reductions. The external building statistics discussed supply market context, rather than results from Spranic's product. The practical demonstration is narrower and concrete: preserve scene observations, compare visits and make spatial evidence available to the people and systems that need it.

episodes.title: Judge a Transaction by the Company It Keeps — Somya Rai & MD Sharique, EXL
episodes.description:
A transaction can look harmless in isolation and suspicious once its links to recent fraud become visible. Somya Rai and MD Sharique explain an EXL fraud detection system that adds graph embeddings to an existing XGBoost classifier. The objective is precision within a fixed analyst alert budget, rather than a better headline score alone. Rai introduces the neighborhood signal and the constraints of two transaction portfolios; Sharique then walks through sampling, graph construction, explanation and serving. They report relative detection improvements of 27% to 33% against their tabular baseline at matched alert rates. The financial figure discussed is projected annualized incremental fraud capture, rather than realized savings.

The engineering decisions start before training. Selected users retain their transaction histories so sampling does not destroy the neighborhoods the model needs. Separate monthly graphs, earlier timestamps and training only preprocessing constrain leakage. GraphSAGE combines mean, maximum and standard deviation, preserving an unusual neighbor that averaging alone could obscure. Attribution connects a suspicious score to specific transaction edges for analyst review. For serving, cached representations and a small online forward pass keep graph sized work off the request path. Moving from transaction node embeddings to user and merchant embeddings reduces the stated cache footprint from roughly 60 GB to 2 to 3 GB. The talk closes with rolling windows, temporal decay and reported millisecond latency, showing the tradeoffs behind the system rather than presenting a universal fraud benchmark.

episodes.title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
episodes.description:
A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs.

Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. The evidence supports a concrete checking workflow, rather than a guarantee that review eliminates every error.

episodes.title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot — Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal, Flywire
episodes.description:
More than 9,700 code review runs in 30 days came from a workflow that lets the model read code but never modify it. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal describe Orbit, Flywire's internal platform for putting model steps inside deterministic engineering workflows. A YAML definition goes through the same merge request review as other code, declares the tools and access each step can use, and runs on the company's existing deployment infrastructure. The predictable work stays in code; a model supplies the judgment. Human review of merge requests remains part of the process as the platform expands across roughly 400 engineers.

Code review, translation updates, dependency fixes, ticket triage and bulk repository changes show the range of tasks this pattern supports. The architecture separates orchestration, execution and session state, then adds timeouts, rate limits and locks against duplicate runs. Per step restrictions cover network access, tools, skills and MCP servers, while structured outputs drive subsequent branches. The speakers are candid about the remaining work: new workflows initially receive a few real case checks, golden datasets run on demand, online evaluations are still being built and full sandboxing is a goal. Their reported execution success rate does not establish answer correctness. The practical adoption path starts with a useful skill, proves the recurring task and then turns it into a background workflow with explicit ownership and review.

episodes.title: Reliable, Smart Workflows for Finance, Wealth and Insurance — Karthic Rao, Perpetual
episodes.description:
“Fill out a form for Mr. Harper” becomes a process that lasts days: identify the right household, find missing information, contact the client, wait, follow up, obtain a signature and retain the evidence. Karthic Rao uses that wealth management example to show why a fixed flowchart breaks on ambiguity and an improvising agent creates a different reliability problem. At Perpetual, his design puts control flow, evidence and external actions in a deterministic system. Models handle interpretation and judgment at explicit, typed points. A judgment can create a smaller plan, but that plan must pass the same compilation and approval boundaries.

The planner translates a request into a semantic graph whose nodes point back to the request. A compiler validates it against the firm's action contracts, returning a valid plan, a clarification request or a refusal. Approved plans are immutable, and external actions have separate gates tied to the exact payload. Waiting and followups are state machine steps; uncertain action outcomes go to manual review rather than automatic retries. Rao shows an illustrative 20 decision run with 19 decisions assigned to a smaller model and one to a frontier model. That ratio is a design target, not a measured fleet result. Typed, logged judgments offer a path toward privately hosted inference and future training, while the training loop remains forthcoming.

episodes.title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI
episodes.description:
A pipeline stripped the minus signs from loan amounts and turned a net $784,000 into $5.3 million of debt, with multiple models agreeing on the wrong result. Hrishi Olickel uses failures like this to explain why transforming data requires more than a universal schema or a confident agent. A customer means something different to billing, support and compliance. Useful structure depends on the source, the storage constraints, the decision being made and the assumptions a model brings to the task. His alternative is a just in time ontology: build the transformation when the question is known, and preserve its context and evidence for reuse.

An Ohio campaign finance entity resolution project provides the working example. Olickel describes separating models that design a pipeline, models that perform its individual jobs and models that optimize the resulting system. Definitions, held out cases and disagreement checks matter as much as model selection. Comparing different model families can concentrate review on their disagreements, but shared assumptions can still produce the same wrong answer. The optimization loop needs a stable execution surface, bounded budgets, reusable methods and a defined way to fail. Small pilots establish a baseline; independently checked work segments make revisions easier to inspect and revert. Only then can the pipeline trade among cost, speed and accuracy without losing the evidence behind its answers.
